title: Engineering OKRs That Measure Real Change
summary: How engineering teams can write OKRs that work: key results as evidence, committed vs aspirational goals, DORA metrics without gaming, and a mid-quarter check-in.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
The planning sheet looks great. Three objectives, nine key results, rows of green cells. Then someone at the end of the table asks the obvious question: if every cell turns green by the end of the quarter, what will actually be better? For users, for the business, for the system we run? The room goes silent for a second. It's an easy question, and nobody wrote the answer down.

That's the trap with OKRs on engineering teams. Used well, they connect the work to a change you can point at. Used badly, they rename the delivery plan as "strategy" and have everyone update percentages until the quarter ends. Here's how to land on the useful side: write key results as evidence, pick the right kind of OKR, choose engineering metrics that won't get gamed, and keep the whole thing alive mid-quarter.

An objective is a direction, a key result is evidence

An objective says where you're heading, in words people will remember during a trade-off. "Make checkout something customers trust." "Get new customers to their first report on day one." "Take the pain out of releases." Specific enough to settle arguments, broad enough that the team can change tactics as it learns.

Key results are where most engineering OKRs go wrong. Google's OKR playbook is blunt about it: key results "must describe outcomes, not activities" (Google's OKR Playbook). It even lists warning words that signal an activity, like "consult", "help", "analyze" and "participate". Compare:

  • "Ship the new retry logic" is a task. "Cut failed checkout attempts by 30% from the June baseline" is evidence.
  • "Write runbooks for the payment service" is a task. "Bring median time to diagnose a payment incident from 40 minutes to 15" is evidence.
  • "Migrate to the new CI runners" is a task. "Keep the main build under 10 minutes for 95% of runs" is evidence.

The numbers above are just examples, so set yours from your own baseline. The point is that a team can close every ticket on the task version while checkout keeps failing exactly as often. The playbook adds one more test worth stealing: scoring 1.0 on all the key results should mean the objective is met. If it wouldn't, a key result is missing.

Say upfront: committed or aspirational?

A lot of OKR anxiety comes from mixing two kinds of goals. The same playbook splits them clearly. Committed OKRs are things the team agrees to deliver, adjusting schedule and resources as needed, and the expected score is 1.0. Aspirational OKRs describe where you'd like to be without a clear path yet, and they have an expected average score of 0.7, with high variance.

Google's re:Work guide puts the sweet spot for grades at 60 to 70 percent, and warns that hitting everything every time suggests the goals weren't ambitious enough (Set goals with OKRs). So label each OKR when you write it. "Keep checkout error rate under 0.5%" during peak season is probably committed. "Halve onboarding time" with no design yet is aspirational. Without the label, a 0.7 on a stretch goal reads as failure, and a 0.7 on a reliability promise reads as fine. Both readings are wrong.

Balance product goals with system health

If every objective is product growth, reliability and maintainability get ignored until the system pushes back, usually during an incident. If every objective is internal cleanup, the team drifts away from what customers notice. A healthy set often has one customer-facing outcome, one reliability or quality outcome, and one capability outcome that makes future delivery easier.

For the delivery side, DORA's metrics are a solid menu: change lead time, deployment frequency, failed deployment recovery time, change fail rate and deployment rework rate (DORA's software delivery metrics). Read the warning on the same page first, though. DORA says setting broad targets on these makes teams more likely to game them, that comparing very different applications can mislead, and that the goal is for each team to improve over time.

Two habits help here. Pair a speed metric with a stability metric, so nobody "wins" deployment frequency by shipping broken changes. And set targets against your own baseline for one service, never against another team's dashboard.

Measurement doesn't have to be perfect, but it has to be honest. Some metrics are noisy, some baselines are partial, some outcomes only show through a proxy. That's fine if the team writes the weakness next to the number. An imperfect key result anyone can inspect beats a vague promise nobody can.

Keep OKRs away from performance reviews

The re:Work guide says plainly that OKRs are not synonymous with performance evaluation. That line matters a lot on engineering teams. Once a key result becomes someone's personal scorecard, people learn to sandbag, hide uncertainty and pick only safe work. And engineering work is full of things nobody controls in a planning meeting: dependencies, discovery, incidents, a vendor changing their API.

Use OKRs to decide what the team focuses on and to learn from what happened. Use separate conversations for how individuals grew. If someone missed an aspirational key result by aiming high and learning a lot, that's the system working.

Check in before the quarter is over

Writing OKRs in week one and grading them in week thirteen is too late to change anything. The re:Work guide says a mid-quarter check-in can be helpful, and some teams revisit a few times a quarter. A good check-in fits in 30 minutes and asks four things:

  • What moved, and what didn't?
  • What did we learn that we didn't know when we wrote this?
  • Is any key result no longer the best evidence for the objective?
  • What should we stop doing?

OKRs protect focus, and they should also give the team permission to adjust when the evidence changes. Changing a key result mid-quarter for a good reason, written down, is a sign the process works. Ignoring it until the retro is a sign it doesn't.

The best part: a better "no"

The real payoff of a good engineering OKR shows up on an ordinary Tuesday. A new request arrives, and the team can ask whether it serves the objective or just feels urgent. Someone proposes a refactor, and it gets tied to a reliability or lead-time outcome instead of being defended as personal taste. Leadership asks for progress, and the team shows a trend line instead of a list of busy weeks.

Try this week

  • Read your current key results out loud and circle any that start with "ship", "build", "migrate" or "help". Rewrite one as evidence.
  • Label every OKR as committed or aspirational, and tell the team what score you expect for each.
  • For any speed metric, add the stability metric that keeps it honest.
  • Put a 30-minute mid-quarter check-in on the calendar now, before the quarter gets busy.

The template doesn't matter much. What matters is the moment an OKR helps the team make a better call than the task list would have. If you can't remember one from last quarter, start with the rewrite above.

faqs.q: What makes a good key result for an engineering team?
faqs.a: A good key result describes a measurable outcome. An activity doesn't count. Google's OKR playbook says key results must describe outcomes and flags words like consult, help, analyze and participate as signs of an activity. 'Ship the new retry logic' is a task. 'Cut failed checkout attempts by 30% from the June baseline' is evidence.

faqs.q: What is the difference between committed and aspirational OKRs?
faqs.a: Committed OKRs are goals the team agrees to deliver, adjusting schedule and resources as needed, with an expected score of 1.0. Aspirational OKRs describe where you'd like to be without a clear path yet, with an expected average score of 0.7 and high variance. Label each one when you write it.

faqs.q: Can DORA metrics be used as key results?
faqs.a: They make a good menu: change lead time, deployment frequency, failed deployment recovery time, change fail rate and deployment rework rate. DORA itself warns that broad targets invite gaming and that comparing very different applications can mislead, so pair speed with stability and set targets against your own baseline.

faqs.q: Should OKRs be tied to performance reviews?
faqs.a: No. Google's re:Work guide says OKRs are not synonymous with performance evaluation. When key results become personal scorecards, people sandbag, hide uncertainty and choose only safe work. Use OKRs for team focus and learning, and keep individual growth for a separate conversation.

faqs.q: How often should an engineering team check its OKRs?
faqs.a: At least once in the middle of the quarter. The re:Work guide says a mid-quarter check-in can be helpful, and some teams revisit a few times a quarter. A 30-minute check-in can ask what moved, what you learned, which key result no longer fits and what to stop doing.
